summary: Small openings in an earbud carry sound, relieve pressure or expose microphones to the outside environment. Protective mesh, vent material, adhesive, paint and assembly position can change those airflow paths. This iSoud guide helps private label buyers ask how an OEM/ODM factory controls acoustic openings from engineering samples through mass-production inspection.

sections.title: Why acoustic openings are part of product performance
body: Gore's TWS acoustic-vent reference describes vent design as part of pressure management and acoustic performance in compact earbuds. Sennheiser maintenance guidance also notes that clogging at the in-ear sound tunnel can reduce sound quality and identifies protective fabric inside the opening. These references show why the visible mesh is not merely decoration.

A private label project may include a nozzle mesh, rear vent, pressure-relief opening and microphone ports, each with a different purpose. Buyers should identify every opening on the drawing and avoid using one generic mesh specification for unrelated airflow paths.

sections.title: Acoustic-mesh RFQ questions for an OEM/ODM factory
bullets: Which openings are for the speaker, pressure relief, rear cavity or microphones?
What mesh or vent material, thickness and airflow specification is assigned to each opening?
How is adhesive applied without reducing the intended open area?
How do paint, printing, coating and decorative parts stay clear of the acoustic path?
Which fixture or measurement compares left and right earbuds after assembly?
How are tilted mesh, excess glue, wrinkles, particles or blocked openings detected?
Which approved sample links the acoustic result to the final custom color and shell process?

sections.title: Adhesive and cosmetic processes need production limits
body: A mesh can use the correct material and still perform inconsistently if it is shifted, folded or covered by excess adhesive. The work instruction should define placement, adhesive boundary, curing, visual acceptance and any airflow or acoustic check used after assembly.

Custom color and surface treatment also belong in the same review. Paint buildup near a vent, decorative printing over a small opening or a changed internal tape can create variation between the engineering sample and the production unit.
bullets: Mark all keep-clear zones on shell and printing drawings.
Use production-intent adhesive and curing conditions for approval samples.
Compare left and right frequency or fixture results against defined limits.
Retain visual reference images for correct mesh position and glue boundary.
Repeat checks after any shell finish, mesh, tape or adhesive change.

sections.title: Maintenance wording should match the selected construction
body: Official product-care pages commonly tell users to keep speaker mesh, air outlets, microphone openings and charging contacts clean without damaging internal protective material. A private label manual should use cleaning instructions approved for the actual mesh, adhesive and shell finish rather than copying a generic method.

faq: What should a buyer ask an earbuds acoustic-mesh factory?
Ask which opening each mesh serves, the material and airflow specification, adhesive controls, cosmetic keep-clear zones, left-right matching limits and production inspection method.
Can excess adhesive change an earbud acoustic opening?
Excess adhesive or shifted mesh can reduce the intended open area, so placement and glue boundaries should be controlled and checked on production-intent samples.
Should custom color be approved separately from acoustic testing?
The final shell finish should be reviewed with the approved mesh, vent, tape and adhesive because cosmetic processes can affect small openings.
